title: Bedfellows Band Calls
prompt: #428: the strange-bedfellows score runs on the device; the founder picks the first band.
context: ADR-0077 §4 settled that Discover's Bedfellows view shows shelf entries from groups that share SOMETHING with you but not EVERYTHING, scored on your device. Nothing is sent or stored. The spike (#428) is built and gated but not pushed: it scored 4 invented readers against 14 invented shelf entries (56 pairs, each marked by hand first). Your picks set the code's defaults and go into an ADR-0077 §4 amendment. All of them stay tunable later, because they're constants and nothing is stored. The full comparison, every pair under every band, is in the spike's bands page, summarized in each decision below.

decisions.title: How likeness is counted
decisions.question: Which way of comparing two texts should the score use?
decisions.summary: Every method here drops filler words ("the", "and"), then counts how much of a shelf entry your own closest Document also says, from 0 (nothing) to 1 (all of it). They differ in whether word endings fold together ("tracking" meets "track") and whether two-word phrases ("public library", "coal plant") count extra. Without the filler list, unrelated pairs scored up to 0.29, so every option keeps it. Pick this first, because the bands below are measured on the recommended method.

options.label: Stems + phrases
options.summary: Fold word endings, and count two-word phrases at twice a word.
pros: Its reasons read well: "okker river", "public library", "opposed war"
Scattered single-word coincidences weigh less
Gap between shared and unrelated: 0.10 vs 0.13
cons: Scores run lower, so the band sits lower
Narrowest margin of the three on these samples

options.label: Stemmed words
options.summary: Fold word endings; every word counts the same.
pros: Catches "schools"/"school", "opposed"/"oppose"
Simple to explain
cons: Folds a chess "boards" into a housing "board": unrelated pairs reach 0.14

options.label: Exact words
pros: Widest gap on these samples (0.10 vs 0.15)
Simplest
cons: Misses every change of form: "tracking" never meets "track"
Its wide gap is partly luck: it happens to miss the boards/board coincidence

decisions.recommendation_reason: It gives the clearest "You both write about …" line, which ADR-0077 requires, and it's the only method whose ranking held up across all four readers. Its smaller numbers just move the band down.

values.stems-phrases: On the device; nothing sent or stored
≈45 ms desktop; ≈0.3 s on a throttled phone profile
A small English stemmer plus phrase pairs

risks.risk: Fourteen invented entries are a small sample; a real shelf may rank differently
risks.mitigation: The amendment sets a trigger: measure again once the pilot shelf holds real entries

risks.risk: The stemmer is English-only; other languages and scripts without spaces score poorly
risks.mitigation: Said plainly in the amendment; revisit if a pilot group writes in another language

examples.title: Porter stemmer
examples.detail: Martin Porter's 1980 suffix-stripping algorithm, the classic way search engines fold "connected" and "connection" together.

examples.title: Lucene's More Like This
examples.detail: Lucene and Elasticsearch find similar documents by term overlap weighted by how distinctive each term is. It's the same family as this method, but runs on a server.

decisions.title: The band: how much in common
decisions.question: Which range of scores should the Bedfellows view show?
decisions.summary: A band is a floor and a ceiling. Above the ceiling is your own kind: near copies of what you already say. Below the floor is noise: coincidences like a chess club's "boards" meeting a housing "board". On the samples, the 7 "shares one thing" pairs score 0.13–0.39, near copies score 0.89–1.00, and unrelated pairs score at most 0.10. One pair mentions one thing only in passing: "coal plant" in one clause, at 0.09. No band takes it in without also taking the boards/winter coincidence at 0.10, so choosing band C is how you'd say passing mentions count.

options.label: A · Close kin 0.20–0.50
options.summary: Only entries sharing a fifth or more of what they say. Shows 4 of 56 pairs.
pros: Nothing shown that shouldn't be
Each match is strong
cons: Misses 3 of 7 "shares one thing" pairs, including the library and the late buses
A small pilot shelf may show nothing at all

options.label: B · Default 0.11–0.50
options.summary: Shares about a ninth or more, and less than half. Shows 8 of 56 pairs.
pros: Takes in all 7 "shares one thing" pairs
Leaves out every near copy and every coincidence
cons: Also shows the hunter × animal-rights pair (see the next decision)
Leaves out the passing "coal plant" mention

options.label: C · Wide 0.08–0.50
options.summary: Lets in passing mentions, and coincidences with them. Shows 10 of 56 pairs.
pros: Takes in the passing "coal plant" pair
More to look at on a small shelf
cons: Shows the boards/winter coincidence: a chess club as kin to a tenants' union
Coincidences make the view feel random

options.label: D · High ceiling 0.11–0.90
options.summary: The default floor, with the ceiling raised until near copies come in. Shows 9 of 56 pairs.
pros: Shows groups very close to you as well
cons: Shows a near copy (0.89): your own kind, not a strange bedfellow

decisions.recommendation_reason: It's the only band that gets every "shares one thing" pair without showing a near copy or a coincidence. Its floor sits in the gap between 0.10 and 0.13, and "less than half" keeps out your own kind.

values.d-high: The opposed pair + a near copy

values.a-close: Two numbers and two sample tests
values.c-wide: Two numbers; two sample tests flip
values.d-high: Two numbers and one sample test

risks.risk: Real shelf entries are longer or shorter than the samples, shifting every score
risks.mitigation: Measure again on the pilot shelf (the amendment's trigger); the band is a constant

risks.risk: The view shows nothing on a small shelf, and people decide it's broken
risks.mitigation: An empty state that says why; widen the floor after the pilot if needed

risks.risk: Coincidences make readers distrust every match
risks.mitigation: The "You both write about …" line shows why; pick a higher floor

risks.risk: Near copies turn Bedfellows into an echo chamber
risks.mitigation: Keep the ceiling at or under 0.5

examples.title: Serendipity in recommender research
examples.detail: Recommender research has long argued that pure accuracy (more of what you already like) narrows what people see. Work on "novelty" and "serendipity" deliberately aims for relevant-but-unexpected, which is what this band is for.

examples.title: The filter bubble
examples.detail: Eli Pariser's 2011 book argued that showing people only what matches them closes them off. A ceiling under 0.5 is a direct answer to that.

decisions.title: Same subject, other side
decisions.question: When an entry is about your subject but takes the other side, does it count as a bedfellow?
decisions.summary: Term overlap can't tell agreement from opposition. On the samples, an animal-rights call to end deer season scores 0.18 against a hunter ("deer, rifles, state, lower, land") and lands in bands B, C and D. Telling sides apart on the device, with no model and no download, isn't reliable. So the real choice is what Discover does about it: show it plainly, ship as is and file a later issue, or let the reader hide entries they don't want.

options.label: Show it as kin
options.summary: Count it: they share a subject, and the "You both write about" line says exactly what.
pros: Hunters and animal-rights groups both care about the deer and the land: a real strange-bedfellows opening
Honest: the reason is on the card
Nothing more to build
cons: Some readers will feel it's the enemy, not a bedfellow

options.label: Ship, file an issue
options.summary: Ship as is, and file an issue to tell sides apart once there's a method that works on the device.
pros: Records the gap so it isn't forgotten
Doesn't block Bedfellows
cons: There may never be a reliable on-device method
Behaves the same as "Show it as kin" until then

options.label: Let readers hide
options.summary: Add a "Not for me" on each Bedfellows entry, remembered only on that device.
pros: The reader decides, not the method
Stays local: nothing sent
cons: New UI and a small local list to keep
A per-device list of hidden groups is itself a record of what someone rejects

decisions.recommendation_reason: Your own words for §4 were "the main goal is still to build strange bedfellows". Two groups that disagree about deer season but both write about the land are the clearest case of that. Because the card says what they share, the reader can judge for themselves.

values.hide: Keeps a local list of hidden entries (high-risk data if seized)
About a day, in the Bedfellows view issue (#433)
A local list, kept and cleared

values.keep: High: add hiding later if the pilot asks
values.hide: Medium: removing it later drops people's hidden lists

risks.risk: A reader sees an opposing group as "kin" and feels misread
risks.mitigation: The card's "You both write about …" line says it's about a shared subject, not a shared stance

risks.risk: A device's list of hidden groups reveals what its owner rejects, if the device is seized
risks.mitigation: Keep it inside the sealed vault, and clear it with the group's data

examples.title: Community Notes' bridging ranking
examples.detail: X's Community Notes shows a note only when people who usually disagree both rate it helpful. Common ground is found across sides on purpose, not filtered out.

examples.title: Polis
examples.detail: Polis groups participants by how they vote, then highlights statements that every opinion group agrees with. Taiwan's vTaiwan process used it.

examples.title: Braver Angels
examples.detail: A US organization that brings people from opposite political sides together around one shared concern at a time.
